title: Personal data; birth and family origins; move to Idaho
description: Isabel Miller fills out a personal data record with Etta Mae Egland, covering her maiden name Knight, her 1905 birth in Peabody, Kansas, and the family's moves through Great Bend and Mount Vernon, South Dakota before coming by train to Grangeville, Idaho in 1918. Her father had worked on the Santa Fe Railroad and she was born in a covered wagon.

title: Aunt Eva; parents' work; siblings
description: Etta Mae describes her aunt Eva Knight of Harrisburg, a postmistress and teacher who unusually adopted a child. She names her mother Mary Elizabeth Stubbs, who cooked and managed restaurants and hotels, her father James Ellsworth Knight, a farmer, union organizer and auctioneer, and her five sisters and brothers.

title: Husband Harry; marriage; children's births and jobs
description: Harry Edward Egland, born in 1895, a lifelong farmer and World War One veteran, joins the interview. The couple describe their 1921 marriage in Asotin, Washington and name their six children with birth dates and current occupations, including a daughter whose husband runs a jewelry store in Aberdeen, Washington.

title: Farm home painting; old Moscow; the Depression
description: While examining a painting on glass of their farm near Moscow, Harry recalls the muddy main street, his mother selling butter and eggs, and five-cent hamburgers. The couple discuss surviving the first depression by selling apples and canning meat, and compare past and present unemployment and welfare.

title: Kansas memories; grandmother's household
description: After learning the interviewer is also from Kansas, Etta Mae recalls Memorial Day parades, her grandmother's roses, and the immaculate house where she was raised. She describes her grandmother's seasonal rug-making, feather beds, and disapproval of her mother's marriage, and her grandfather being paid three hundred dollars to serve in the Civil War.

title: John's diabetes; family size and birth control
description: Etta Mae tells how her son John nearly died before being diagnosed with severe diabetes, leading her to suspect her grandfather's starvation death was undiagnosed diabetes. She and the interviewer then discuss how women of her grandmother's generation limited their families.

title: Joan's sewing; army life; Portland shop plans; remaining children
description: Etta Mae describes daughter Joan's life as an army colonel's wife in Germany, Nepal, Thailand and Korea, her skilled sewing, and the couple's plans to retire in Portland with a shop selling jewels and mounted screens. She also gives birth dates and jobs for sons Michael James and John Hans.

title: Etta Mae's schooling; canning; butchering; farm women's work
description: Etta Mae recounts her two years of high school and her life as a farm wife: canning dozens of quarts of food, butchering hogs with help from the Christensen brothers, making sausage, lard, soap and butter, cooking three meals plus two field lunches daily, and sewing for the children.

title: Pea-packing job; visitors; hobbies; clubs and church
description: Etta Mae describes her one winter working at a green pea packing plant in Moscow after World War Two. Her daughter Irma and granddaughter Hollis arrive, and she then lists her holiday craft hobbies, her clubs in Moscow and Genesee, and her offices in the women's group of Valley Lutheran Church.

title: Views on rural life, generations, opportunities and marriage
description: Etta Mae reflects on the advantages of farm life for raising children, the freer relationship she fostered compared with her strict upbringing, and the greater opportunities young women have now. She recalls marrying Harry in 1921 without much reflection and her deep loneliness as a young farm wife, and the interviewer asks how she met her husband.

title: Courtship; wedding; marriage expectations
description: Etta Mae Egland describes meeting her husband Harry in Moscow, Idaho, their courtship from March to October, and their wedding in Asotin. She reflects on how young she was and how well the marriage turned out.

title: Childbirth; hospital experiences
description: Etta Mae and Harry recount the births of their six children, including Harry's role administering ether during the first birth and a memorable incident when their Model T truck broke down while Etta Mae was in labor with their son Wally.

title: 50th anniversary trip; children
description: The couple describes their trip to Washington, D.C., for their 50th wedding anniversary, visiting historical sites and seeing where the old hospital had been replaced by the United Nations building.

title: Financial security; reading habits; advice for young women
description: Etta Mae discusses never worrying about money, the newspapers and magazines they read, and her belief that electricity was the biggest improvement in farm life.

title: Electricity; loneliness; farm work
description: Etta Mae reflects on the arrival of electricity on the farm, her feelings of loneliness as a young bride unprepared for farm life, and her acceptance of the work, including washing clothes on a board.

title: Television; radio; milking; household division of labor
description: The couple discusses their TV and radio habits, Harry's skill as a milker, and how they divided responsibilities—she ran the house while he managed the outside work.

title: Finances; decision to move to town
description: Etta Mae explains their joint bank account and describes the decision to move into town, motivated by their son John's diabetes and the demands of school activities, despite Harry's initial reluctance.

title: Family size; reflections; Depression
description: She reflects on having six children without planning them, whether she would have done anything differently, and how they coped during the Depression.

title: 50th anniversary celebration; release form
description: Etta Mae describes their 50th wedding anniversary party at church with over 200 guests, and signs the release form for the interview.

title: Family history; generational differences
description: She expresses regret about not knowing more about her parents and grandparents, contrasting her own reluctance to ask questions with her grandchildren's curiosity about family history.
